content: Pain is a defining feature of sickle cell disease (SCD), often presenting as severe, frequent, and unpredictable episodes. While nociceptive pain is more common, individuals with SCD may also experience neuropathic pain, which arises from injury to peripheral or central nerves. This review specifically focuses on the treatment of painful sensory neuropathy in individuals with SCD. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of pharmacological and non-pharmacological therapies for managing neuropathic pain in people with SCD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, trial registries, and reference lists of relevant articles. Experts in the field were also consulted. The last search was performed on January 31, 2019. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and studies comparing pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions to placebo or other treatments. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for eligibility, extracted data, evaluated the risk of bias using the Cochrane risk of bias tool, and rated the quality of evidence using GRADE guidelines. Only one RCT, conducted in the United States with 22 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either pregabalin (n=11) or placebo (n=11). Pregabalin was administered orally, starting at 75 mg twice daily, with titration up to a maximum of 600 mg daily or reduction by 75 mg per day based on clinical presentation and pain levels. Neuropathic pain was assessed using self-reported measures, including the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs (S-LANSS) scale and the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI), where higher scores indicated greater pain severity. Outcomes such as pain relief, quality of life, and withdrawal due to adverse effects were measured at baseline and monthly for three months post-intervention. The overall risk of bias in the trial was low, although there was a high risk of bias due to participant attrition. Regarding the primary outcome of self-reported neuropathic pain relief, the evidence was of very low quality, and the results were inconclusive. At the end of three months, there was no clear difference between the pregabalin and placebo groups as measured by the S-LANSS scale (mean difference [MD] -2.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] -9.18 to 5.18) or the NPSI scale (MD -11.10, 95% CI -33.97 to 11.77). The trial did not report on the 'Patient Global Impression of Change' outcome. Quality of life, assessed using the Short Form-36 (SF-36) questionnaire, showed small improvements in seven of the eight domains in the pregabalin group compared to the placebo group at three months. However, this evidence was also of very low quality, and it remains uncertain whether pregabalin improves quality of life. Pre-defined outcomes such as 'time to improvement of symptoms' and 'changes in sleep quality' were not measured in the trial. Adverse effects appeared to be more frequent in the pregabalin group compared to the placebo group at three months, but the evidence was of very low quality, and the difference was uncertain (relative risk [RR] 1.33, 95% CI 0.39 to 4.62). One participant in the pregabalin group withdrew due to adverse effects, while three participants in the placebo group withdrew or dropped out due to adverse effects, complications, or hospitalization related to SCD. In conclusion, the single included trial provided very low-quality evidence. While self-reported pain relief was greater in the pregabalin group compared to the placebo group using the S-LANSS scale, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether there is a true difference. Similarly, while the pregabalin group showed a trend toward improved quality of life, the evidence remains inconclusive. Adverse effects and withdrawal rates were comparable between the pregabalin and placebo groups. Overall, there is a significant lack of evidence regarding interventions for neuropathic pain in individuals with SCD, highlighting the need for further research in this area.
